title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents
summary:
CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today. 
 The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents . Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday , called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.
 Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”
 CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall , both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic , began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers . The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
summary:
Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

 First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

 Explicit lazy imports 
 I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so:

 lazy import json 
 lazy from pathlib import Path 
 The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

 My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

 Unpacking in comprehensions 
 The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation :

 lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]]
[ * L for L in lists ]
 # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 
 # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] 

 sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }]
{ * s for s in sets }
 # {1, 2, 3, 4} 
 # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} 

 dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }]
{ ** d for d in dicts }
 # {'a': 3, 'b': 2}

title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
summary:
At a glance 

 StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers

 AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale 

 StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student 

 The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance 

 Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor 

 In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies

title: web-edit 0.1a0
summary:
Release: web-edit 0.1a0 

 I was working on a project from my phone using Codex Remote when I found myself wanting to edit a credentials file without round-tripping those credentials through the LLM itself.

 So... I had Codex and GPT-6 Astra Extra High build this Python web app which provides a web UI for viewing and editing files in a folder. It's intended to be run over Tailscale, so I can have an agent start this running and then edit files via my Tailscale network directly from my phone.

title: Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are considered to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) evaluation. With MT evaluation spanning a large number of language pairs, domains and levels of annotation granularity, LLMs must be thoroughly evaluated across these dimensions before being reliably used as alternatives to human evaluation. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human…

title: Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
summary: The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing…

title: Self-Compacting Language Model Agents
summary: Long agent traces composed of chains of thought and tool calls accumulate stale content that anchor subsequent generations, and eventually outgrow the context window. Existing scaffolds mitigate it with fixed-interval compaction triggered at a token threshold. Such triggers pay no heed to trajectory structure, risking discard of partial results mid-derivation or mid-search. We propose SELFCOMPACT, a scaffold that allows the model itself to decide when and how to compact.
